motd: Welcome to Amonel OS. Type help to see every command - or start with about, skills or projects.

commands.ask: put a question to the Assistant, e.g. ask Where does Ahmadreza work?
commands.troubleshoot: open the Network app's fault-finding game: the office's internet is down
commands.ls: list files, ls -a shows hidden ones too
commands.cd: change directory, cd .. goes up one level

help.keys: Tab completes commands and paths, arrow up and down bring back earlier commands, Ctrl+L clears the screen, Ctrl+C abandons the line.

amonel.name: Amonel - this website
amonel.text: 80 years of computing history in seven eras, each with a puzzle that teaches a real foundation of computing - and this desktop at the end. A static website without a server of its own, in German, English and Persian.

ask.handoff: Passing your question to the Assistant.
ask.usage: Ask the Assistant straight from the terminal: ask followed by your question, for example ask Where does Ahmadreza work?

eggs.moth: The first "bug" was real: on 9 September 1947 technicians taped a moth from relay 70 of the Harvard Mark II into the logbook. We have been hunting them ever since.
eggs.sl: Mistyped ls? This train leaves on time anyway.
eggs.coffee: According to RFC 2324 a teapot may not brew coffee. For real coffee: the contact command.
eggs.rm: Nice try. This file system is read-only - just like history.
eggs.editor: Don't worry, nobody gets trapped in an editor here. cat reads any file.
eggs.hire: Excellent idea. The contact command shows how to reach Ahmadreza, and cv what he brings.
eggs.uptime: Counted from ENIAC, 1946 - the first era of this journey.
eggs.ping: A browser may not send real packets. The Network tools show how ping answers - as an honest simulation.

fortune.0: The eight-bit byte became the standard with IBM's System/360 in 1964.
fortune.1: The first word sent over a network was "lo": in 1969 the ARPANET crashed at the "g" of "login".
fortune.2: 640 KB ought to be enough - whether anyone really said so has never been shown.
fortune.3: The mouse was first called an "X-Y position indicator for a display system".
fortune.4: A ping across the Atlantic takes at least as long as light needs in glass.
fortune.5: UNIX time counts seconds from 1 January 1970.
fortune.6: The cloud is just someone else's computer - with very good air conditioning.

legends.header: Every era has two sourced facts - insider and legend:

eniac.insider: Anyone programming with punch cards drew a diagonal line across the top of the deck with a felt-tip pen. If the deck was dropped, the line showed which card went where.
eniac.legend: ENIAC computed in decimal, not binary. It was programmed by plugging cables and setting switches - rewiring for a new problem could take days. Of its roughly 17,500 tubes, most failed right at power-on or power-off, so the machine was rarely switched off.

batch.insider: The IBM 704 had sense switches: toggle switches on the console that a running program could read. In FORTRAN that was IF (SENSE SWITCH 3) - the operator could steer a program without stopping it.
batch.legend: "Chad" is the term for the small paper bits punched out of a card. A mispunched hole meant wrong data - or a jammed card reader.

unix.insider: Up to the Sixth Edition, the command for changing directory was called chdir. The short cd only arrived in 1979 with the Seventh Edition.
unix.legend: Unix time counts seconds since 1970-01-01, 00:00 UTC. Stored in a signed 32-bit counter, it overflows on 2038-01-19 at 03:14:07 UTC.

dos.insider: In MS-DOS, F3 brought back the last command line you typed. If you knew that, you never typed a long command twice.
dos.legend: The 640 KB limit came from the IBM PC's memory map: the upper 384 KB of its 1 MB address space were reserved for video memory and ROM. The quote "640K ought to be enough for anybody" is unverified - Bill Gates has denied ever saying it. People tuned CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT to reclaim what they could.

macintosh.insider: The ⌘ symbol on the Command key is Susan Kare's. She found it in a book of symbols: in Sweden it marks places of interest on signs.
macintosh.legend: Susan Kare drew the first Mac icons on graph paper, one square per pixel, before digitizing them.

win95.insider: To see your IP address on Windows 95, you typed winipcfg into Start › Run. Today's ipconfig did not exist there.
win95.legend: A PC had 16 IRQ lines; two devices sharing one could crash the system. Windows 95's Plug and Play earned the nickname "Plug and Pray" for it.

cloud.insider: On Linux, only root may open ports below 1024. That is why so many containers listen on port 8080 instead of 80.
cloud.legend: "Works on my machine" is answered by containers: Docker, launched publicly in 2013, ships an app together with its whole runtime environment.

bsod.title: Amonel OS ran into a problem
bsod.message: Someone probably tried to move the mouse pointer with a punch-card command. Nothing is lost - not even this session.
bsod.dismiss: Any key, a click or Esc brings you back.

man.name: AMONEL(1)
man.description: An interactive journey through 80 years of computing history, followed by a desktop with Ahmadreza's portfolio. Seven eras, seven puzzles, one goal: show how computers actually work.

lo.explain: On 1969-10-29, a UCLA student tried to send the word LOGIN to a computer at Stanford. The receiving machine crashed after two letters - "LO" was the first message ever sent over a computer network.
